title: Can a private chef cook for a family with different diets?
body_markdown:
Yes. A private chef can cook for a family with different diets by planning shared meal components and preparing separate dishes where requirements conflict. For a Dubai household, the key is a written brief covering each person’s restrictions, preferences and portions. Allergies and medically prescribed diets need additional discussion before you agree the menu or kitchen arrangements.


**TL;DR**

- For a private chef managing multiple diets in a Dubai family, agree individual requirements before approving a shared menu.
- myCHEF provides private chef services and weekly meal prep; discuss your household’s dietary requirements before booking.
- Shared components suit compatible preferences; separate preparation needs its own agreed process.
- An ingredient substitution alone does not resolve allergen cross-contact risks.


## Can a private chef cook for a family with different diets?

**Yes, but the menu must account for each person rather than treating the household as having one diet.** Start with what everyone can eat, then identify which components need changing and which meals require separate preparation.

A vegetarian adult, a meat-eating adult and a child who prefers mild food do not necessarily need unrelated dinners. A shared vegetable dish, separate proteins and sauces served individually can create a meal that still feels shared. This approach works only when the ingredients and preparation arrangements meet everyone’s requirements.

For a closer look at specific dietary requests, read the guide to [keto and gluten-free meals with a private chef](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-a-private-chef-cook-keto-or-gluten-free-meals-in-dubai). Use it to identify questions for your brief, not as confirmation that every kitchen can accommodate every restriction.

### A practical comparison of menu approaches

| Approach | Best for | Main benefit | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shared base, separate additions | Compatible preferences and different protein choices | Keeps much of the meal in common | Shared ingredients still need checking |
| Adapted versions | Families wanting similar dishes with different ingredients | Preserves a familiar meal format | Substitutions can change flavour and texture |
| Separate meals | Requirements that do not fit the same recipe | Allows distinct menus | Adds preparation, equipment and storage needs |

These are planning approaches, not advertised packages. Ask the chef which approach fits your household before treating a sample menu as agreed.

## Why a written dietary brief matters

A label such as healthy, dairy-free or low-carb leaves important questions unanswered. Does dairy-free describe a preference or an allergy? Does low-carb mean avoiding bread at dinner, or following targets supplied by a dietitian?

**Record the actual requirement, not just the diet name.** A useful brief separates food exclusions, medical instructions, religious requirements, dislikes and portion preferences. That distinction helps the chef understand what can be adjusted and what must not change.

Keep household rules separate from individual requests. If an ingredient must not enter the kitchen, say so explicitly. If someone simply prefers a sauce on the side, record that without presenting it as a safety restriction.

## How should you brief a chef about different diets?

Prepare a person-by-person record before discussing recipes. You do not need a long document, but everyone responsible for approving meals should work from the same version.

1. **Name the requirement.** Identify whether it is an allergy, diagnosed condition, religious requirement, preference or dislike.
2. **Describe the exclusions.** List ingredients to avoid rather than relying entirely on a broad dietary label.
3. **Explain acceptable alternatives.** Record substitutions the person already eats and any they reject.
4. **Describe portions and timing.** Explain who eats each meal, whether meals are shared and who reheats food later.
5. **Agree the boundaries.** Confirm what the chef can accommodate, what needs separate preparation and what remains unresolved.

The last step matters as much as the menu. A chef should not have to infer whether a shared utensil, substitute ingredient or last-minute change is acceptable.


![Dietary briefing steps from naming requirements to agreeing preparation boundaries](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/08568400-b68d-4148-9f1f-0aa072ed1617/body-07ad0c0368a5a00a486686cbdee2195f.jpg)

*Agree the preparation boundaries before approving the menu.*


Keep the final brief somewhere the household can update. If a requirement changes, communicate the change directly and obtain confirmation before the next cooking session. Do not assume a conversation with one family member has reached everyone involved.

## Can everyone eat versions of the same dinner?

Yes, when the ingredients and preparation methods are compatible. Building a meal from components lets you change a protein, accompaniment or seasoning without redesigning every plate.

The following is an **illustrative menu structure, not a myCHEF menu or a guarantee of dietary suitability**:

- A vegetable component with its ingredients agreed in advance.
- A plant-based protein and a separately prepared meat or fish option.
- A grain or other accompaniment selected around the household brief.
- Dressings, garnishes and stronger seasonings served separately.

This structure gives the chef a starting point. It does not establish that the meal is suitable for a particular allergy, coeliac disease or prescribed diet. Those requirements need ingredient and preparation checks beyond the dish name.

Ask for the complete recipe description when reviewing an adaptation. Replacing a main ingredient is only part of the decision: stocks, marinades, sauces and garnishes also belong in the discussion.

### When separate meals make more sense

Separate meals are appropriate when adapting a shared dish would undermine the requirement or make the result unappealing. They also give you a clearer way to organise genuinely different meal times or individual menus.

The trade-off is practical. Separate dishes need their own preparation sequence and enough equipment and storage. Confirm that the proposed cooking session covers those tasks rather than assuming additional meals fit automatically.

## What changes when someone has a food allergy?

A food allergy requires a different conversation from a preference. Avoiding an ingredient in the recipe does not, by itself, address allergen cross-contact through hands, utensils, equipment or surfaces.

Before agreeing a service, discuss:

- The specific allergen and the individual’s established instructions.
- Ingredient labels and how substitutions will be checked.
- Shared equipment, utensils and preparation surfaces.
- Food storage and separation within the household kitchen.
- Who confirms that the proposed arrangements are acceptable.

**Do not accept a general dietary-friendly description as confirmation that an allergy can be accommodated.** Ask for a clear answer about the actual kitchen and cooking process. If those arrangements cannot meet the person’s requirements, choose a different arrangement.

The chef’s role is food preparation, not diagnosis or treatment. Where a clinician or registered dietitian has issued instructions, share those instructions rather than asking the chef to interpret symptoms or create a treatment plan.

## How do you handle children’s meals and adult preferences?

Start by identifying what genuinely needs to differ. A child’s preference for mild seasoning does not necessarily require a separate main dish, while a different texture preference can require a more substantial change.

Discuss familiar foods, disliked textures and how the family serves meals. Serving sauce separately or keeping components distinct gives the chef a clear direction without promising that a child will accept every dish.

Portion planning deserves its own conversation. Avoid treating every family member as an identical adult portion, and distinguish food intended for dinner from food reserved for lunch the following day.

If family members eat at different times, agree how their meals will be set aside and identified. The person serving dinner should not have to guess which container belongs to whom or whether a garnish is suitable.

## Why does the preparation involved vary between families?

The workload depends on how requirements interact, not simply how many dietary labels appear in the enquiry. Compatible preferences can share preparation; conflicting restrictions need a more detailed plan.

Discuss these factors when comparing proposals:

- **Ingredient overlap:** whether family members can share bases, sauces and accompaniments.
- **Separate preparation:** whether dishes need distinct equipment, utensils or work areas.
- **Menu variety:** whether the brief repeats familiar meals or requests frequent recipe changes.
- **Portions and meal coverage:** who needs breakfast, lunch, dinner or food for later.
- **Kitchen facilities:** available cooking equipment, preparation space and refrigeration.
- **Packing and serving:** whether meals are served immediately or divided into individual containers.

Ask what the proposal includes and excludes. Shopping, ingredients, containers, washing up and meal labelling should be confirmed individually; none should be assumed from the phrase private chef.

myCHEF provides vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep. That identifies the relevant service category, but your proposed menu, preparation arrangements and inclusions still need agreement for your household.

## What should you check in your Dubai kitchen?

Describe the kitchen as it is, including any limitations. Tell the chef about available hob and oven space, refrigeration, usable utensils and areas that cannot be used for particular ingredients.

Access arrangements belong in the same brief. Explain building entry procedures, parking or unloading arrangements and any household timing restrictions. Ask what equipment the chef expects to use rather than assuming everything arrives with them.

Think beyond the cooking session. If meals remain in your fridge, leave room for the agreed containers and establish a labelling system that everyone understands. Household members should know which meals are theirs before the chef leaves.

Finally, identify who approves substitutions. If an ingredient is unavailable, the chef needs a clear contact and an agreed decision process—not competing instructions from different family members.

## How should you assess a proposed family menu?

Review the menu person by person, not just dish by dish. A varied menu can still leave someone without a complete meal if their only suitable component is a side dish.

Use this checklist before approving it:

- Every person has a suitable main meal, not merely an omitted ingredient.
- Sauces, garnishes and accompaniments match the relevant restrictions.
- Substitutions are named rather than left open-ended.
- Separate preparation requirements are acknowledged.
- Portions and meals reserved for later are identified.
- Unresolved questions are answered before cooking begins.

Ask what happens if the menu needs changing after approval. Confirm how changes are communicated and accepted, without assuming a particular notice period or booking policy.

**Approve the meal plan and preparation process together.** A recipe list tells you what will be cooked; the process tells you whether it fits your household.

## FAQ


**Can a private chef cook vegetarian and meat dishes for the same family?**

Yes, a private chef can plan vegetarian and meat dishes within the same household menu. Agree which components can be shared and which need separate ingredients or preparation.

**Can a private chef accommodate a food allergy at home?**

Accommodation depends on the specific allergy and the kitchen arrangements. Discuss ingredients, shared equipment, storage and cross-contact before booking; a suitable recipe alone is not enough.

**Do different diets mean everyone needs a separate meal?**

No, compatible requirements can use shared components with different additions. Separate meals are appropriate when substitutions or shared preparation would not meet the agreed brief.

**Can children have smaller portions and milder food?**

You can request different portions and milder seasoning in the household brief. Confirm textures, ingredients and serving arrangements rather than assuming an adult meal simply needs reducing.

**Can a chef follow a dietitian’s meal instructions?**

Ask the chef to review the dietitian’s written instructions before accepting the service. Confirm whether the required ingredients, measurements and preparation methods can be followed; the chef does not replace clinical advice.

**What should I send when enquiring about family meal preparation?**

Send your location, preferred dates, number of people and the meals you need prepared. Add each person’s dietary requirements, relevant kitchen limitations and whether you want recurring cooking or a single occasion.

- [Can meal-prep portions be adjusted for children?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-meal-prep-portions-be-adjusted-for-kids)
- [Do private chefs bring groceries and equipment?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-bring-their-own-groceries-and-equipment)

## Plan the household brief before the recipes

The most useful starting document is not a favourite menu. It is a clear account of who needs what, which ingredients cannot be used and how meals will be prepared and served.

For a tailored myCHEF enquiry, send your preferred date or recurring schedule, Dubai location, guest or household count and service required. Include each person’s dietary requirements and ask for confirmation of the proposed cooking arrangements before approving your menu.
